hints: Look at the displayed structure of glycolic acid and list the two different oxygen containing functional groups it contains.
Recall which reagent gives effervescence of $\text{CO}_2$ only with acids stronger than carbonic acid.
Recall what type of carbonyl compound gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, and check if glycolic acid contains that group.
Recall the colour change when acidified $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ oxidises a primary or secondary alcohol.
walkthrough:
Spot the two reactive groups in glycolic acid**
You have $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$. That is both a carboxylic acid ($\text{COOH}$) and a primary alcohol ($\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) in the same molecule. Each test reagent probes for a different group, so think about them one at a time.

Carbonate tests the acid group**
Carboxylic acids are strong enough to react with carbonate to release $\text{CO}_2$ gas: $2\text{RCOOH} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{RCOONa} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. So you see effervescence or bubbling. Tick for reaction, functional group is $\text{COOH}$.

2,4-DNPH tests for aldehyde or ketone carbonyl**
2,4-DNPH gives an orange-yellow precipitate only with an aldehyde or ketone $\text{C=O}$. Glycolic acid has a carboxylic acid $\text{C=O}$, not an aldehyde or ketone, and an alcohol $\text{C-OH}$. So there is no visible reaction. Cross for no reaction.

Acidified dichromate tests the alcohol group**
Acidified $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ is an oxidising agent that oxidises primary and secondary alcohols, itself being reduced from orange $\text{Cr(VI)}$ to green $\text{Cr(III)}$. The $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ group is a primary alcohol, so you see orange to green. Tick for reaction, functional group is $\text{OH}$ / alcohol.

Final answer: $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\text{(aq)}$: effervescence / fizzing, reaction occurs ✓, due to $\text{COOH}$ / carboxylic acid.
2,4-DNPH: no visible reaction / no precipitate, no reaction ×.
Acidified $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$: orange to green, reaction occurs ✓, due to $\text{OH}$ / primary alcohol.

hints: Recall that $\text{HCN}$ adds across the $\text{C=O}$ of an aldehyde to add $\text{H}$ to O and $\text{CN}$ to C.
walkthrough:
Build the cyanohydrin from methanal**
Start with $\text{HCHO}$. Addition of $\text{HCN}$ across the $\text{C=O}$ gives $\text{H}_2\text{C(OH)CN}$. Draw a carbon with two $\text{H}$ atoms, one $\text{OH}$ group and one $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ group. That is 2-hydroxyethanenitrile, intermediate $\text{X}$.
Final answer: Displayed structure of $\text{HOCH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$: central C bonded to $\text{H}$, $\text{H}$, $\text{OH}$ and $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$.

hints: Think what type of hydrolysis converts a $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ group into a $\text{COOH}$ group in reaction 2.
walkthrough:
Recognise nitrile to acid hydrolysis**
$\text{X}$ contains $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ and the product contains $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. Hydrolysis of a nitrile to a carboxylic acid needs aqueous acid, such as dilute $\text{HCl}$ or dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, usually with heating.
Final answer: Dilute hydrochloric acid / dilute sulfuric acid / dilute nitric acid, heated.

hints: Recall the mechanism name when $\text{Br}_2$ substitutes a $\text{C-H}$ hydrogen in an alkane or alkyl group.
walkthrough:
Link $\text{Br}_2$ substitution to radicals**
Reaction 3 replaces a $\text{C-H}$ hydrogen in $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ by $\text{Br}$ to give $\text{CH}_2\text{BrCO}_2\text{H}$. Substitution by bromine in the absence of a polar mechanism is free-radical substitution.
Final answer: Free-radical substitution.

hints: Think what energy source is needed to split $\text{Br}_2$ into $\text{Br}$ radicals to start the chain.
walkthrough:
Supply energy for homolysis**
Free-radical substitution is initiated by homolytic fission of $\text{Br-Br}$ into $2\text{Br}^\bullet$. That needs UV light or sunlight.
Final answer: UV light / sunlight.

hints: Identify the nucleophile and its lone pair, and the electrophilic carbon attached to Br.
Recall the two curly arrows for SN2: nucleophile to carbon, and $\text{C-Br}$ bond to Br, with correct $\delta+$ and $\delta-$ labels.
walkthrough:
Set up the nucleophilic attack**
$\text{OH}^-$ is the nucleophile. Put a lone pair on the O and draw a curly arrow starting at that lone pair and pointing to the carbon of the $\text{C-Br}$ group. That carbon is electron poor because Br pulls electrons away, so label it $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ and Br as $\text{Br}^{\delta-}$.

Break the carbon bromine bond**
As the new $\text{C-OH}$ bond forms, the old $\text{C-Br}$ bond breaks. Draw a second curly arrow starting at the $\text{C-Br}$ bond and pointing onto Br to give $\text{Br}^-$. This single concerted step with backside attack is the $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism.

Final answer: Curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{OH}^-$ to $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of $\text{C-Br}$; $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ dipole shown; curly arrow from $\text{C-Br}$ bond to $\text{Br}$ to form $\text{Br}^-$.

hints: Look at what happens to the aldehyde group in glyoxylic acid: it gains hydrogen to become an alcohol.
walkthrough:
See reduction by gain of hydrogen**
The aldehyde $\text{CHO}$ group in glyoxylic acid becomes $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ in glycolic acid. Gain of hydrogen is reduction, so $\text{NaBH}_4$ donates hydrogen and acts as a reducing agent.
Final answer: Reducing agent / reductant.

hints: Count atoms to write the molecular formulae of glyoxylic acid ($\text{OHC-CO}_2\text{H}$) and glycolic acid ($\text{HOCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$).
Balance the gain in H atoms using $\text{[H]}$ on the left hand side.
walkthrough:
Write the two molecular formulae**
Glyoxylic acid $\text{OHC-COOH}$ is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_3$. Glycolic acid $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$ is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_3$. The carbon and oxygen counts are already the same.

Balance with [H]**
The product has two more H atoms than the reactant, so add $2\text{[H]}$ on the left: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{[H]} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_3$$ This shows reduction clearly.

hints: Recall the two broad O-H absorptions expected for glycolic acid: one for the carboxylic acid and one for the alcohol.
Look at spectrum Y between 1500 and 4000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ and check for absence of very broad bands around 2500-3000 and 3200-3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Predict what glycolic acid should show**
Glycolic acid has two $\text{OH}$ types. The carboxylic acid $\text{O-H}$ gives a very broad band at 2500-3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$, and the alcohol $\text{O-H}$ gives a broad band at 3200-3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$.

Read spectrum Y in that region**
In spectrum Y from 1500 to 4000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ you see sharp $\text{C-H}$ peaks near 2900-3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ and a strong $\text{C=O}$ near 1750 $\text{cm}^{-1}$, but no very broad $\text{O-H}$ humps at 2500-3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ or at 3200-3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. The missing bands prove both $\text{OH}$ groups have been lost during formation of Y.

Final answer: Spectrum Y lacks the very broad absorption at 2500-3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{RCO}_2\text{-H}$ and lacks the broad absorption at 3200-3650 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{RO-H}$. Therefore Y contains no $\text{OH}$ groups.

hints: Use the equation $2\text{CH}_2\text{(OH)CO}_2\text{H} \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_4\text{O}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to deduce that two ester links form with loss of water.
Think how two molecules each with one $\text{OH}$ and one $\text{COOH}$ can join head to tail twice to make a six-membered ring with two $\text{COO}$ groups.
walkthrough:
Work out that esters must form**
Two glycolic acid molecules lose $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to give $\text{C}_4\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$. Loss of water between $\text{OH}$ and $\text{COOH}$ means esterification. Since part (d)(i) shows no $\text{OH}$ remains, both $\text{OH}$ groups and both $\text{COOH}$ groups must have reacted to give two ester groups.

Join two molecules into a ring**
Let the $\text{OH}$ of molecule 1 esterify the $\text{COOH}$ of molecule 2, and the $\text{OH}$ of molecule 2 esterify the $\text{COOH}$ of molecule 1. You get a six-membered ring: $\text{-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-O-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)-O-}$ closed back on itself. That is the cyclic diester 1,4-dioxane-2,5-dione.

Final answer: Cyclic diester (glycolide): six-membered ring of alternating $\text{CH}_2$ and ester groups, 1,4-dioxane-2,5-dione, containing two $\text{COO}$ ester linkages, molecular formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_4\text{O}_4$.
